Bradley Steyn [5477]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
15th of November 1988 South Africa teeters on the edge of a state of emergency. Seventeen-year-old Bradley Steyn crosses Pretoria’s Strijdom Square and walks straight into a massacre. Barend Strydom, the notorious white supremacist ‘Wit Wolf’, is mowing down black bystanders relaxing in the square during their lunch break. Bradley cradles a dying man in his arms and, later, with reports of eight dead and 16 seriously injured, he is brought face-to-face with the insanity of the nation.
Suffering from acute PTSD, unable to cope with day-to-day life and consumed by rage, Bradley spirals out of control. His parents unwittingly initiate the next chapter in the story of the boy who crossed the square when they arrange for him to join the SA Navy.

Here, angry and unable to work though his trauma, he is called on by the apartheid regime’s Security Branch to ‘confront the threat of communism’, and the navy serviceman joins the dreaded D Section of the Security Branch as a classified government enforcer – but not for long as the underground ANC’s Department of Intelligence and Security (DIS) soon recruits him.
On the political stage events are changing fast: FW de Klerk becomes president, the ANC is unbanned and Nelson Mandela walks to freedom. However, undermining this progress, a sinister Third Force has formed an alliance between the deep state military-intelligence complex, the neo-Nazis and the white supremacists. With these forces edging the nation towards a bloody race war, De Klerk is forced to make a deal with Mandela. Bradley is part of the DIS’s plan to infiltrate this Third Force network before all hope for a free future is destroyed. He goes undercover to help unravel the extremists’ master plan. At this time, Bradley was recruited by Jeremy Vearey and Andre Lincoln, from the ANC’s Department of Intelligence and Security (DIS) in the early 1990’s as an infiltration asset inside the then Security Police. Through the information that he is able to supply the ANC, many of the Third Force Projects are thwarted.
His cover is blown just before independence and an attempt was made on his life, he was advised by his handlers to leave the country immediately.

These experiences have profoundly changed his life. Steyn now lives in California. He works as a security consultant in Beverley Hills.

Although Strijdom Square has now been renamed to Lilian Ngoyi Square, 30 years later Brad is still determined to find survivors of the massacre and have a commemoration plaque installed to honour those who lost their lives.


People to interview options;

8 Minutes 1 day shoot. Brad Steyn interview and stock footage. Will need at least 3 minutes stock footage.
Strijdom Park Massacre, End of Apartheid, Right Wing Factions, World Trade Centre and 30 Year Comemoration.

10 minutes 2 day shoot. Brad Steyn and ANC Handlers. Johannesburg and Cape Town. Plus Stock as above.

Script:


Brad Steyn Final Script
V/O
When Nelson Mandela was inaugurated in 1994, few knew that surrounding the podium was specially reinforced ballistic glass to prevent an assassination attempt on his life.

Jeremy: “A specially built 50 calibre sniper’s rifle was intended to be used to take out Madiba.
And it was a plot that was heating up and heating up and closer to the time of the inauguration it required definitive defensive measure with the glass that we had.”

V/O
Major General Jeremy Veary, was one of Mandela’s bodyguards and an ANC counter intelligence operative during the liberation struggle.
In the 90’s, he met an aggressive young Afrikaans man looking for answers - his name was Bradley Steyn. Veary knew that he could be useful, and recruited him.

Jeremy: “In Brad’s life I was his handler as part of the ANC’s department of intelligence and security and was involved in directing him to collect and gather information from the security police infiltrate right wing organisations such as WAM.”

V/O
Bradley’s new book Undercover With Mandela’s Spies explores the barbaric events that has largely been forgotten. It’s the story of the boy who crossed the Strijdom square on the 15th of November 1988.

Brad: “As I was walking in this direction that when I saw people panicking and scattering and that’s when I saw this guy in his camouflage fatigues walking with a 9mm in his hand.”

V/O
23 year old former policeman Barend Strydom or the Wit Wolf as he was later called, was on a mission to kill every black person he encountered on the streets of Pretoria in the name of white supremacy. He went on a shooting spree, killing 8 black people and injuring 16 more. Just 17 at the time, the events that Bradley witnessed have haunted him since.

Brad: “Then I noticed him walk up to a black person and lift the gun and he shot them in cold blood in front of me.”

Link
It was total mayhem, people were running in all directions trying to get away from the lone gunman, but Bradley recalls that surreal moment when he noticed Barend Strydom had a smile on his face.


Brad
“I was probably about 6-8 m in front of him”

Brad
“I heard to my left psst psst Klein baas and I looked to my left and I saw a young black guy, and then he called me, so I looked to see if it was safe and I jumped up and I ran over the bench and I was lying behind the bench with him ….

V/O
They were terrified and then Strydom killed another person nearby…

Devi
“But what happened after that?”

Brad
“So he’s a few steps ahead of me and I soon as I come around the corner, I see Strydom pointing his gun at him and shooting him. Strydom sees someone running towards him, lifts his forearm and points in my direction . I assume that because I was white, he lowered the firearm.

Devi
“So Barend Strydom them speaks directly to you?”

Brad
“I said to him hoekom doen jy dit? Why are you doing this? And he said he was doing it for the future of white South Africans.”

V/O
That day also changed Feroz Carrim’s life.

V/O His father, Satar Abdool Carrim had a shop in Pretoria. Feroz was helping him at the store and had stepped out of the shop, when he came back 15 min later his world had altered irreparably.

Feroz
“…. this guy came down shooting from church square and then he came in front of my father’s store and then he shot the lady in front of my father’s shop and he shot another two people and then my father came out from his counter and they had a confrontation. And when he shot, he shot my father through the hip.”



V/O
Feroz’ father died a week later, but he still lives with the loss.

Devi
“It brings it all back hey?
Every day.”

V/O
Barend Strydom was eventually overpowered and arrested but he left a trail of devastation and loss… Bradley remembers holding a young man in his arms. He was shot in his chest and was struggling to breathe.

Brad
‘I took my fingers and tried to put them in the bullet holes to stop the blood from pumping out but he was coughing and gasping

V/O
Major General Veary was in prison for terrorism at the time the massacre took place. He believes that these killings shifted the consciousness in the country.

Jeremy
“And that seems to have been a watershed moment where the white community was confronted with the extreme form of what they all grew up under….”

V/O
Barend Strydom was sentenced to death but was released 4-years later as part of the liberation talks between the ANC and the Apartheid Government.

Steyn says he does not know what happened to young man who protected him or any of the other victims of the atrocity. But what he does know is that what he witnessed that day changed him. He started working as a bouncer for nightclubs – a job that turned out to be just a front for something far more sinister.

Brad
‘The next thing I knew I was working for the security police in the western cape and doing all their dirty work for them.”

Brad
“My tug of war with the morality of what was right and what was wrong was fragmented, it was almost as if I was put into a mindset specifically to go and hunt and find, kick doors down and stop the communist threat.”

V/O
Steyn believes that his aggression was a result of the post-traumatic stress disorder he developed after the Strydom massacre.

Brad
“Its haunted me you know, its part of the ptsd that I still suffer today. If I happen to be asleep and I wake up. The first thing that comes to mind for me is that there’s a threat.
I wake up and I want to kill somebody….

V/O Steyn says that while working for the Security Branch he realized that he wasn’t protecting the country from the communist threat but that he was part of the oppressive regime. He started to gain clarity when an ANC cadre he was ordered to interrogate, reached out to him… years later… Veary made covert contact with him - the movement needed spies inside the apartheid government, and Steyn seemed to be the solution but they had to be sure…

Veary: “Through small tests, getting information here and getting chicken feed like we call in the trade craft, whether the person is prepared to take the risk to get that information. Through those small series of tests you determine you are dealing with a person who is able to do the job.


Link
On the political stage events were changing fast. FW de Klerk became president, the ANC was unbanned and Nelson Mandela was about to walk to freedom as South Africa’s first democratically elected president.

V/O
Over time Steyn proved his value to the ANC. Veary deployed him to infiltrate the World Apartheid Movement a militant right wing organisation, that was far more extreme than the Afrikaaner Weerstandbeweging or AWB.

Veary: “If you want to target those elements, it comes with a calculated risk of exposure that means death, these guys don’t play, the same applies to inside the security police. They had a different way of dealing with people that came with fatal consequences.”

V/O
Steyn’s cover was eventually blown and he was told there was a hit out on his life. He fled to America and became a security specialist. Years later, he would return to South Africa….


Link
Strijdom Square was demolished and a new square named after ANC activist Lilian Ngoyi was built but no where here is there any mention of those people who were massacred on that day.

V/O
In the National Archives Bradley has searched through police reports to find any clues about the surviving families whereabouts.That is how he found Feroz and his family.

Feroz
“If you go to his tombstone, it says to the world he was a father to us he was the world.

V/O
In November this year, on the 31st anniversary of the massacre, Bradley hopes to erect a plaque at Lillian Ngoyi Square and bring all of the families together to acknowledge all those who died on that fateful day.

Feroz
“We have to commemorate these people, we have to understand that their sacrifice their lives without undersstanding that they made a difference in the emotions of others that made the change in the difference of the change in this country. So ja, you have to recognise them.



Promos – 11 seconds…

• Former apartheid police operative and later a spy for Umkhonto we Sizwe - Bradley Steyn is still haunted by the Strydom Square massacre he witnessed over thirty years ago. Now he’s on a mission to honour those who died on that fateful day.
• Revealing secrets of a dirty war in the dying days of apartheid, former apartheid police spy and Umkhonto we Sizwe operative Bradley Steyn recalls the Strijdom Square massacre that motivated his career in intelligence.
• After witnessing the Strydom Square massacre as a teenager, Bradley Steyn is still haunted by the events that lead to the death of eight people at the hands of the so-called Wit Wolf, Barend Strydom.
